hints: Look at what changes from phenylethanoic acid to R, the $\text{-OH}$ of the $\text{-COOH}$ group is replaced by $\text{-Cl}$ to give $\text{-COCl}$.
walkthrough:
Spot the functional group change**
You start with $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ and you end with $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{COCl}$. Only the $\text{-OH}$ part of the carboxylic acid has been swapped for $\text{-Cl}$. This is the classic preparation of an acyl chloride.

Recall the specialist chlorinating reagents**
Carboxylic acids do not react with $\text{HCl}$ to give acyl chlorides. You need a more powerful reagent that can replace $\text{-OH}$ by $\text{-Cl}$. Any one of phosphorus(V) chloride $\text{PCl}_5$, phosphorus(III) chloride $\text{PCl}_3$ or thionyl chloride $\text{SOCl}_2$ does this job.
Final answer: $\text{PCl}_5$ or $\text{PCl}_3$ or $\text{SOCl}_2$

hints: Focus on the new $\text{-CONH-}$ linkage in S, with $\text{C=O}$ directly attached to N.
walkthrough:
Read the linkage in S**
In S you have $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CONHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The carbonyl carbon $\text{C=O}$ is now bonded directly to nitrogen. That $\text{-CONH-}$ group is the defining feature of an amide.

hints: Balance atoms between $\text{R + C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ and S, the $\text{Cl}$ from $\text{-COCl}$ and one H from the amine must go somewhere.
walkthrough:
Track the lost atoms**
Think of it as $\text{-COCl + H-NHCH}_2\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{-CONHCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{HCl}$. The $\text{Cl}$ leaves the acyl chloride and the H leaves the amine nitrogen. Together they form hydrogen chloride $\text{HCl}$.

Allow for the basic amine**
In practice the $\text{HCl}$ formed is immediately neutralised by a second molecule of the basic ethylamine to give the salt ethylammonium chloride, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_3\text{Cl}$. Either $\text{HCl}$ or this salt is accepted as the other product.
Final answer: $\text{HCl}$ or $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_3\text{Cl}$

hints: Compare S and T, the $\text{C=O}$ of the amide becomes $\text{CH}_2$ in the amine, so oxygen is removed and hydrogen is added.
walkthrough:
Recognise a difficult reduction**
You are converting $\text{-CONH-}$ to $\text{-CH}_2\text{NH-}$. The carbonyl oxygen is completely removed. This is reduction of an amide to a primary or secondary amine.

Choose the strong enough hydride**
Mild reducing agents such as $\text{NaBH}_4$ or $\text{H}_2$ with Ni cannot reduce amides. You need the powerful hydride donor lithium aluminium hydride, $\text{LiAlH}_4$, in dry ether followed by acid work up.

hints: Decide whether oxygen is lost or gained and whether hydrogen is gained or lost on going from $\text{-CONH-}$ to $\text{-CH}_2\text{NH-}$.
walkthrough:
Apply the oxygen and hydrogen test**
Going from S to T, the molecule loses oxygen from the $\text{C=O}$ and gains hydrogen to make $\text{CH}_2$. Loss of oxygen plus gain of hydrogen is reduction.

hints: Recall ethylamine $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ contains 2 carbon atoms, and each $^{13}\text{C}$ contributes about 1.1% of the M peak intensity.
walkthrough:
Link M+1 to carbon-13**
The small M+1 peak is almost entirely due to molecules containing one $^{13}\text{C}$ instead of $^{12}\text{C}$. Natural abundance of $^{13}\text{C}$ is about 1.1% per carbon atom.

Scale by number of carbons and M intensity**
Ethylamine has formula $\text{C}_2\text{H}_7\text{N}$, so 2 carbons. $$\text{abundance of M+1} = 2 \times 1.1\% \times \text{abundance of M}$$ $$= 2 \times 1.1 \times 0.62 = 1.36$$ This gives about 1.4 to at least 2 significant figures.
Final answer: relative abundance $= 2 \times 1.1 \times 0.62 = 1.36$ (about 1.4)

hints: For $m/e = 29$, look for a small alkyl fragment from the ethyl side chain of T that adds to 29.
For $m/e = 91$, look for the very stable benzyl fragment from cleavage next to the phenyl ring, $\text{C}_7\text{H}_7^+$.
walkthrough:
Assign m/e 29**
Compound T is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Cleavage of the ethyl group gives the ethyl cation. Mass $= 2(12) + 5(1) = 29$. So the ion is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^+$.

Assign m/e 91**
Cleavage at the benzylic position gives the very stable benzyl cation. Mass $= 7(12) + 7(1) = 91$. So the ion is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2^+$, often drawn as the phenyl ring plus $\text{CH}_2^+$.
Final answer: $m/e$ 29: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^+$ ; $m/e$ 91: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2^+$

hints: Recall which type of proton appears well downfield, around $\delta$ 7, due to the ring current.
walkthrough:
Match shift range to environment**
Protons on a benzene ring are strongly deshielded and appear at $\delta$ about 6.5 to 8.0. In the labelled structure only protons a are on the phenyl ring. All alkyl $\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{NH}$ protons appear below $\delta$ 5. So the answer is a.

hints: Think about which proton is attached to a heteroatom (N) and can rapidly exchange with deuterium.
walkthrough:
Find the exchangeable proton**
Proton d is the $\text{N-H}$ proton of the secondary amine. $\text{N-H}$ and $\text{O-H}$ protons exchange with $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ to give $\text{N-D}$ which gives no proton NMR signal. So the peak for d disappears. $\text{C-H}$ protons b, c, e, f and aromatic a do not exchange.

hints: Use the n+1 rule and remember proton d causes no splitting, so only count neighbouring C-H protons on adjacent carbons.
walkthrough:
Apply n+1 ignoring the N-H**
You are told d does not split c or e. So count only C-H neighbours. Proton b ($\text{PhCH}_2$) is next to 2 H on c, so $2+1 = 3$, triplet. Proton c ($\text{CH}_2$N) is next to 2 H on b, so $2+1 = 3$, triplet. Proton f ($\text{CH}_3$) is next to 2 H on e, so $2+1 = 3$, triplet. Proton e ($\text{NCH}_2$) is next to 3 H on f, so quartet. Hence triplets are b, c and f.
Final answer: b, c, f

hints: The most shielded protons are furthest from electronegative N and from the phenyl ring.
walkthrough:
Compare distance from deshielding groups**
Nitrogen and the phenyl ring both withdraw electron density and deshield nearby protons, moving them to higher $\delta$. Proton f is the terminal $\text{CH}_3$ of the ethyl group, furthest from both N and the ring and bonded only to carbon and hydrogen. It is the most shielded, so it has the lowest $\delta$, typically around 1.
